title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a case of a model asserting fabricated information as fact, occurring at the document-preparation stage of legal practice. An attorney used an AI tool called Irys to help draft court filings, and the tool generated seven case citations across eight filings that did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and invented quotations. The fabrications were caught not by the filing attorney but by opposing counsel, meaning no internal verification step intercepted the errors before they reached the court.

The specific failure mode is AI hallucination applied directly to legal citation, a context where every reference must correspond to a real, retrievable document. The attorney believed the tool was integrated with her firm's legal research subscription and would verify citations automatically. That belief was mistaken, and no separate manual check was performed. Catching this earlier would have required the attorney to verify each citation independently against an authoritative legal database before filing.

What is not established is whether the tool itself made any representation about being connected to a citation-verification service, or whether that assumption arose entirely on the attorney's side.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized in court after their legal filings contained fabricated cases, quotes, and legal holdings created by artificial intelligence. The errors were discovered by attorneys representing Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, a Los Angeles homeowner suing State Farm and others over delays in rebuilding her home after a 2020 fire in Carson. Attorney Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions and confirmed seven case citations across eight filings that did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and quotes. Robinson mistakenly believed the tool was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription and would check citations automatically.

The lawsuit stems from significant damages to Meni-Siliga's family, who lost their home to foreclosure after being unable to complete repairs due to storm damage and delays in getting State Farm's approval. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident reflects a broader trend of legal hallucinations across the industry, with databases tracking nearly 1,900 such cases worldwide. State Farm stated it expects its external counsel to maintain the highest ethical standards, while the legal profession increasingly adopts AI tools, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments now using generative AI.
